quotes.Resolution 31312: In 2011, the Mayor and City Council adopted a bold climate protection goal for our community to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed the creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312). The resulting 2013 Climate Action Plan (CAP) provided a coordinated strategy aimed at reducing GHG emissions while also supporting other community goals, including building vibrant neighborhoods, fostering economic prosperity, and enhancing racial and social justice. The 2013 CAP included a slate of near-term actions - many of which were completed by 2015 - and more broadly defined longer-term strategies to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.
quotes.Resolution 31757: In response to the Trump administration's withdrawal of support for the international Paris Climate Agreement last year, the City Council adopted Resolution 31757, affirming Seattle's commitment to the goals established in the Paris Agreement, and directing the Office of Sustainability & Environment (OSE) to identify the actions necessary to do our part to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The resulting actions, developed under the leadership of Mayor Durkan, reflect a tipping point in the transition to Seattle's zero emissions future. They are designed to move beyond incremental change and fundamentally reshape our building and transportation systems for a fossil fuel-free future.
quotes.In 2017, the Seattle Electrical Code was: In 2017, the Seattle Electrical Code was amended to ensure new parking is built to facilitate future electric vehicle charging infrastructure. The code requires adequate electrical capacity to serve one electric vehicle charging station per parking space and that construction documents show the location of equipment and conduit for future installation of electric vehicles charging stations.
quotes.Adopted in 2010, Seattle's Energy Benchm: Adopted in 2010, Seattle's Energy Benchmarking Program (SMC 22.920) requires owners of nonresidential and multi-family buildings (20,000 square feet or larger) to track energy performance and annually report to the City. The policy was updated in 2016 to make reported data publicly available to further increase awareness of building energy use and support real estate market transformation. It is estimated that Seattle's benchmarked buildings represent about two-thirds of citywide commercial and industrial square footage. The Benchmarking and Transparency policy is foundational to reducing energy use and GHG emissions - raising the awareness of energy consumption among building owners and managers enables opportunities to reduce energy use and save money. The data also helps the City track overall building energy use and emissions while informing energy efficiency policy and program development. Program staff assist building owners with compliance, ensure data quality is high, and connect customers to rebates and technical assistance. Seattle has an industry leading compliance rate of 99 percent each of the past four years. Since 2014, buildings benchmarking three consecutive years have demonstrated a 2.7 percent decrease in energy use.
quotes.Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups O: Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019.  A Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist is required to complete the assessment, report to the City, and monitor implementation of operational and maintenance improvements. Examples of operational fixes include changes to thermostat set points, or adjusting lighting or irrigation schedules. Tune-ups also review HVAC, lighting, and water systems to identify needed maintenance, cleaning or repairs. These types of improvements typically reduce individual building energy use an estimated 10-15 percent. Across the entire commercial building sector, the tune-up mandate is expected to reduce energy use 5-8 percent and GHG emissions by 6-9 percent.
quotes.committed (Resolution 31652) to meeting: To demonstrate leadership, build capacity in the industry, and help reduce compliance costs, the city has committed (Resolution 31652) to meeting the Building Tune-Ups deadline one year earlier than required for private owners.
quotes.the City is implementing the Building Tu: With funding from a Department of Energy grant, the City is implementing the Building Tune-Up Accelerator Program providing incentives for early compliance with the Tune-Ups Ordinance. The Accelerator is a voluntary program for owners of mid-size buildings, those 50,000-100,000 square feet, to conduct a tune-up that meets the Seattle Building Tune-Up requirements in advance of when their building is required to comply (2020 & 2021). Building owners can receive Seattle City Light incentives for the tune-up and will be encouraged to go beyond a tune-up by conducting additional energy conservation measures. The University of Washington Integrated Design Lab is providing no-cost technical support and guidance for owners pursing more extensive energy upgrades. Participating energy service providers will perform building assessments and assist owners in meeting the tune-up requirements, as well as collect building characteristic data and work with owners to pursue additional energy-savings opportunities.
quotes.In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Con: In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491), with the goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 (2008 baseline). The Office of Sustainability & Environment manages the dedicated funding and works with individual capital departments to prioritize, develop and implement energy efficiency projects. The City is on track to meet the reduction goal, with a 12 percent energy use reduction through the end of 2016.
quotes.goal to reduce municipal fleet emissions: Seattle was one of the first cities in the country to buy conventional hybrids (early 2000s) and the battery electric Nissan Leaf (2011), install hybrid systems on ambulances, and use a 20 percent biodiesel blend from sustainable feedstocks in all heavy-duty vehicles. The Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to meet the goal to reduce municipal fleet emissions by 50 percent by 2025 by increasingly electrifying the fleet, using cleaner fuels when electrification is not feasible, increasing efficiency in how vehicles are used, and setting standards for vehicle procurement. The City's fleet includes over 200 electric vehicles and over 300 hybrid vehicles. Between 2013 and 2016, GHG emissions from the municipal fleet decreased by 11.5 percent and total fuel use decreased by five percent.

quotes.Adopt a tiered state residential energy: Adopt a tiered state residential energy code that can be adopted by cities.
quotes.Legislation to allow for tiered energy c: Cities are currently only able to adopt a commercial energy code in Washington state, while the state controls the residential version. Seattle and other municipalities are interested in a tiered residential energy code, which would allow them to adopt an incrementally higher standard. State legislation would be required directing the State Building Code Council, which Seattle is a member of, to develop the tiered code. Higher tiers could also be used as the base State code in the following code cycle. Legislation to allow for tiered energy codes will be a priority for the City of Seattle in the 2019 legislative session.
quotes.Create pilot program offering additional: Create pilot program offering additional height and floor area incentives for significant upgrades in energy and water use, and transportation efficiency.
quotes.Provide programs and incentives to spur: Provide programs and incentives to spur improved energy efficiency and reduced carbon emissions, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030.
quotes.Scale Pay for Performance efforts and pi: Scale Pay for Performance efforts and pilot an innovative utility program exploring Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings to unlock greater levels of energy efficiency depth at scale.
quotes.Seattle City Light will pilot Energy Eff: Seattle City Light will pilot Energy Efficiency as a Service (EEaS), which is explicitly designed to help participants overcome the split incentive barrier in commercial buildings, where there is little motivation for a building owner or investor to finance deep energy retrofits whose benefits accrue to tenants. EEaS lets investors finance projects with a predictable return, owners generate a new revenue stream, and tenants occupy productive and energy efficient spaces. The pilot will leverage the lessons learned from a prototype at the Bullitt Center.
quotes.Double existing budget allocation for re: Double existing budget allocation for reducing energy in municipal buildings from 2012-2015, with a goal of reducing energy use by 40 percent.
quotes.the City will double its budget allocati: City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio. Building on existing efforts to reduce energy use 20 percent by 2020, the City will double its budget allocation from 2021 to 2025, and set a new target to achieve an overall 40 percent energy and carbon emissions reduction in municipal buildings by 2025.
quotes.OSE will propose recommendations to the: OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.

all_policies.policy_statement: By October 2018, the Mayor of Seattle will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with City departments to define which projects to assess for GHG impacts, the assessment method, and how to account for broader carbon costs.
all_policies.source_quote: City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.  However, the City lacks a systematic way to assess the GHG emissions associated with major City actions, and to consider the cost of those emissions during the planning process. Creating such a system would help the City make better decisions in the short-term and be prepared for future financial impacts, such as carbon pricing. The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.

Seattle has an industry leading compliance rate of 99 percent each of the past four years. Since 2014, buildings benchmarking three consecutive years have demonstrated a 2.7 percent decrease in energy use.

dedup.policy_statement: Seattle’s Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930), adopted in 2016, requires commercial buildings ≥50,000 square feet to identify low- or no-cost operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency, with phased compliance deadlines beginning in early 2019; it also requires a Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist to complete and report the assessment and monitor implementation.
dedup.source_quote: Adopted in 2016, the Building Tune-Ups Ordinance (SMC 22.930) requires commercial buildings 50,000 square feet or larger to identifying low- or no-cost building operations and maintenance improvements to improve energy and water efficiency. Compliance deadlines will be phased in by building size, beginning in early 2019.  A Qualified Tune-Ups Specialist is required to complete the assessment, report to the City, and monitor implementation of operational and maintenance improvements. Examples of operational fixes include changes to thermostat set points, or adjusting lighting or irrigation schedules. Tune-ups also review HVAC, lighting, and water systems to identify needed maintenance, cleaning or repairs. These types of improvements typically reduce individual building energy use an estimated 10-15 percent. Across the entire commercial building sector, the tune-up mandate is expected to reduce energy use 5-8 percent and GHG emissions by 6-9 percent.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is an adopted ordinance establishing mandatory building tune-ups with a stated phased compliance start date.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle committed via Resolution 31652 to meet the Building Tune-Ups deadline for City buildings one year earlier than the deadline required for private owners.
dedup.source_quote: To demonstrate leadership, build capacity in the industry, and help reduce compliance costs, the city has committed (Resolution 31652) to meeting the Building Tune-Ups deadline one year earlier than required for private owners.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a formal City commitment anchored in a resolution with a clear schedule acceleration (one year earlier), though the specific deadline date is not stated in the quote.

dedup.policy_statement: With funding from a U.S. Department of Energy grant, the City of Seattle is implementing the Building Tune-Up Accelerator Program to provide incentives for early compliance with the Tune-Ups Ordinance for owners of mid-size buildings (50,000–100,000 square feet) ahead of required compliance in 2020 and 2021.
dedup.source_quote: With funding from a Department of Energy grant, the City is implementing the Building Tune-Up Accelerator Program providing incentives for early compliance with the Tune-Ups Ordinance. The Accelerator is a voluntary program for owners of mid-size buildings, those 50,000-100,000 square feet, to conduct a tune-up that meets the Seattle Building Tune-Up requirements in advance of when their building is required to comply (2020 & 2021). Building owners can receive Seattle City Light incentives for the tune-up and will be encouraged to go beyond a tune-up by conducting additional energy conservation measures. The University of Washington Integrated Design Lab is providing no-cost technical support and guidance for owners pursing more extensive energy upgrades. Participating energy service providers will perform building assessments and assist owners in meeting the tune-up requirements, as well as collect building characteristic data and work with owners to pursue additional energy-savings opportunities.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is an implementation commitment backed by an identified funding source (DOE grant) and a specific program mechanism (incentives for early compliance) with stated compliance years.

dedup.policy_statement: In 2013, the City of Seattle adopted the Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491) with the goal of achieving a 20% reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 from a 2008 baseline.
dedup.source_quote: In 2013, the City adopted a Resource Conservation Management Plan (Resolution 31491), with the goal to achieve a 20 percent reduction in energy use across City-owned buildings by 2020 (2008 baseline). The Office of Sustainability & Environment manages the dedicated funding and works with individual capital departments to prioritize, develop and implement energy efficiency projects. The City is on track to meet the reduction goal, with a 12 percent energy use reduction through the end of 2016.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is an adopted resolution with a quantified municipal energy-reduction target, deadline, and baseline.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities.
dedup.source_quote: Announce that the City will develop and release a strategy to address congestion and transportation emissions through pricing, coupled with investments in expanded transit and electrification in underserved communities.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a City commitment to produce and release a strategy; it specifies the mechanism (pricing) and accompanying investment focus but does not give a release date in the commitment sentence.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018 to ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure.
dedup.source_quote: Pass a new electric vehicle readiness ordinance in 2018, which will ensure new construction or renovation of parking structures is built with electric vehicle infrastructure.
dedup.section_header: Electric vehicle readiness ordinance for new construction
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a legislative commitment (pass an ordinance) with a stated year (2018) and defined scope (new construction/renovation of parking structures).

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will release a map of the optimal distribution of electric vehicle charging infrastructure in 2018.
dedup.source_quote: Release map of optimal distribution of charging infrastructure in 2018.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a time-bound City deliverable (release a map in 2018) intended to guide charging infrastructure deployment.

dedup.policy_statement: The Mayor of Seattle will issue an Executive Order directing City departments to assess the GHG emissions impacts of City plans, policies, and major investments.
dedup.source_quote: Issue an Executive Order directing City departments to assess the GHG emissions impact of City plans, policies, and major investments.
dedup.section_header: Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a clear executive action (issue an Executive Order) that creates an administrative requirement for departments.

dedup.policy_statement: By the end of 2018, the City of Seattle will create a new Green Fleet Action Plan to accelerate electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
dedup.source_quote: Create a new Green Fleet Action Plan, by the end of 2018, to accelerate the electrification of the municipal fleet and phase out fossil fuel use in municipal vehicles.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a time-bound City commitment to produce a new plan with explicit decarbonization objectives for municipal vehicles.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will pursue adoption of a tiered Washington State residential energy code that cities can adopt.
dedup.source_quote: Adopt a tiered state residential energy code that can be adopted by cities.
dedup.section_header: Washington State tiered residential energy code
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is framed as an adoption commitment but refers to a state code; the City’s role is to pursue/advocate rather than unilaterally enact, and no adoption date is specified.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will make legislation to allow tiered residential energy codes a priority in the 2019 Washington State legislative session.
dedup.source_quote: Cities are currently only able to adopt a commercial energy code in Washington state, while the state controls the residential version. Seattle and other municipalities are interested in a tiered residential energy code, which would allow them to adopt an incrementally higher standard. State legislation would be required directing the State Building Code Council, which Seattle is a member of, to develop the tiered code. Higher tiers could also be used as the base State code in the following code cycle. Legislation to allow for tiered energy codes will be a priority for the City of Seattle in the 2019 legislative session.
dedup.section_header: Washington State tiered residential energy code
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a concrete government commitment to pursue state legislation in a specified session (2019).

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will create a pilot program offering additional height and floor area incentives for significant upgrades in energy and water use, and transportation efficiency.
dedup.source_quote: Create pilot program offering additional height and floor area incentives for significant upgrades in energy and water use, and transportation efficiency.
dedup.section_header: Establish new 2030 Challenge pilot for 20 upgraded, high performing projects by 2025
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a City commitment to create an incentive pilot; the heading references 'by 2025' and '20 projects' but those specifics are not contained in the quoted commitment line.

dedup.policy_statement: The City of Seattle will provide programs and incentives to improve energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions in commercial and multifamily buildings, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030.
dedup.source_quote: Provide programs and incentives to spur improved energy efficiency and reduced carbon emissions, backed by a minimum performance standard beginning in 2030.
dedup.section_header: Incentive-driven 2030 performance standards for commercial and multifamily buildings
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a clear commitment to implement a minimum performance standard with a start date (2030) and supporting programs.

dedup.policy_statement: Seattle City Light will scale Pay for Performance efforts and pilot an Energy Efficiency as a Service utility program in up to 30 buildings.
dedup.source_quote: Scale Pay for Performance efforts and pilot an innovative utility program exploring Energy Efficiency as a Service in up to 30 buildings to unlock greater levels of energy efficiency depth at scale.
dedup.section_header: City Light Whole Building Pay for Performance (P4P) Programs
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a utility program commitment including a quantified pilot scope (up to 30 buildings).

dedup.policy_statement: Seattle City Light will pilot Energy Efficiency as a Service (EEaS) to address split incentives in commercial buildings.
dedup.source_quote: Seattle City Light will pilot Energy Efficiency as a Service (EEaS), which is explicitly designed to help participants overcome the split incentive barrier in commercial buildings, where there is little motivation for a building owner or investor to finance deep energy retrofits whose benefits accrue to tenants. EEaS lets investors finance projects with a predictable return, owners generate a new revenue stream, and tenants occupy productive and energy efficient spaces. The pilot will leverage the lessons learned from a prototype at the Bullitt Center.
dedup.section_header: City Light Whole Building Pay for Performance (P4P) Programs
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is an explicit pilot implementation commitment; it overlaps with the up-to-30-buildings item but provides the direct 'will pilot EEaS' language, so it is kept as a distinct but related policy statement.

dedup.policy_statement: From 2021 to 2025, the City of Seattle will double its budget allocation for reducing energy in municipal buildings and set a target to achieve an overall 40% reduction in energy use and carbon emissions in municipal buildings by 2025.
dedup.source_quote: City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio. Building on existing efforts to reduce energy use 20 percent by 2020, the City will double its budget allocation from 2021 to 2025, and set a new target to achieve an overall 40 percent energy and carbon emissions reduction in municipal buildings by 2025.
dedup.section_header: Improve municipal building energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions by 2025
dedup.extraction_rationale: This includes a resource commitment (budget doubling) plus a quantified municipal target with a deadline (2025).

dedup.policy_statement: Seattle’s Office of Sustainability & Environment will propose recommendations to the Mayor to accelerate the conversion of 18,000 homes from heating oil to electric heat pumps, including a financing plan for low-income residents and public/private incentives.
dedup.source_quote: OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a department-level commitment to deliver formal recommendations with a quantified scope (18,000 homes) and named mechanisms (financing plan and incentives), though it does not state a deadline for the recommendations.

dedup.policy_statement: By October 2018, the Mayor of Seattle will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with City departments to define which projects to assess for GHG impacts, the assessment method, and how to account for broader carbon costs.
dedup.source_quote: City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.  However, the City lacks a systematic way to assess the GHG emissions associated with major City actions, and to consider the cost of those emissions during the planning process. Creating such a system would help the City make better decisions in the short-term and be prepared for future financial impacts, such as carbon pricing. The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.
dedup.section_header: Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions
dedup.extraction_rationale: This is a time-bound mayoral directive to a named office to establish the scope and method for a GHG assessment system by a specified deadline.

dedup2.policy_statement: In 2011, the Mayor of Seattle and Seattle City Council adopted a community climate protection goal to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312).
dedup2.source_quote: In 2011, the Mayor and City Council adopted a bold climate protection goal for our community to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed the creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312). The resulting 2013 Climate Action Plan (CAP) provided a coordinated strategy aimed at reducing GHG emissions while also supporting other community goals, including building vibrant neighborhoods, fostering economic prosperity, and enhancing racial and social justice. The 2013 CAP included a slate of near-term actions - many of which were completed by 2015 - and more broadly defined longer-term strategies to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.
dedup2.extraction_rationale: This is an adopted City resolution establishing a quantified community-wide target (carbon neutral by 2050) and directing plan creation.

dedup2.policy_statement: Seattle City Council adopted Resolution 31757 affirming Seattle’s commitment to the Paris Agreement goals and directing the Office of Sustainability & Environment to identify actions needed to limit warming to 1.5°C.
dedup2.source_quote: In response to the Trump administration's withdrawal of support for the international Paris Climate Agreement last year, the City Council adopted Resolution 31757, affirming Seattle's commitment to the goals established in the Paris Agreement, and directing the Office of Sustainability & Environment (OSE) to identify the actions necessary to do our part to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The resulting actions, developed under the leadership of Mayor Durkan, reflect a tipping point in the transition to Seattle's zero emissions future. They are designed to move beyond incremental change and fundamentally reshape our building and transportation systems for a fossil fuel-free future.
dedup2.extraction_rationale: This is an adopted City Council resolution that both affirms targets and issues a directive to a named department.

dedup2.policy_statement: In 2017, the City of Seattle amended the Seattle Electrical Code to require new parking to include adequate electrical capacity for one electric vehicle charging station per parking space and to require construction documents to show equipment and conduit locations for future EV charging installation.
dedup2.source_quote: In 2017, the Seattle Electrical Code was amended to ensure new parking is built to facilitate future electric vehicle charging infrastructure. The code requires adequate electrical capacity to serve one electric vehicle charging station per parking space and that construction documents show the location of equipment and conduit for future installation of electric vehicles charging stations.
dedup2.extraction_rationale: This is an amended code with enforceable requirements for EV-ready electrical capacity and documentation.

dedup2.policy_statement: The City of Seattle’s Green Fleet Action Plan guides actions to reduce municipal fleet greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2025 through electrification, cleaner fuels where electrification is not feasible, efficiency in vehicle use, and procurement standards.
dedup2.source_quote: Seattle was one of the first cities in the country to buy conventional hybrids (early 2000s) and the battery electric Nissan Leaf (2011), install hybrid systems on ambulances, and use a 20 percent biodiesel blend from sustainable feedstocks in all heavy-duty vehicles. The Green Fleet Action Plan guides the City's efforts to meet the goal to reduce municipal fleet emissions by 50 percent by 2025 by increasingly electrifying the fleet, using cleaner fuels when electrification is not feasible, increasing efficiency in how vehicles are used, and setting standards for vehicle procurement. The City's fleet includes over 200 electric vehicles and over 300 hybrid vehicles. Between 2013 and 2016, GHG emissions from the municipal fleet decreased by 11.5 percent and total fuel use decreased by five percent.
dedup2.extraction_rationale: This includes a quantified municipal target (50% by 2025) tied to an established City plan guiding implementation; specific measures are described but funding is not specified.

dedup2.extraction_rationale: This is an explicit pilot implementation commitment; it overlaps with the up-to-30-buildings item but provides the direct 'will pilot EEaS' language, so it is kept as a distinct but related policy statement.

dedup2.policy_statement: From 2021 to 2025, the City of Seattle will double its budget allocation for reducing energy in municipal buildings and set a target to achieve an overall 40% reduction in energy use and carbon emissions in municipal buildings by 2025.
dedup2.source_quote: City-owned buildings comprise four percent of commercial building area of the city. The City will lead the way toward performance standards by aiming to reduce energy and emissions from our own building portfolio. Building on existing efforts to reduce energy use 20 percent by 2020, the City will double its budget allocation from 2021 to 2025, and set a new target to achieve an overall 40 percent energy and carbon emissions reduction in municipal buildings by 2025.
dedup2.section_header: Improve municipal building energy efficiency and reduce carbon emissions by 2025
dedup2.extraction_rationale: This includes a resource commitment (budget doubling) plus a quantified municipal target with a deadline (2025).

dedup2.policy_statement: Seattle’s Office of Sustainability & Environment will propose recommendations to the Mayor to accelerate the conversion of 18,000 homes from heating oil to electric heat pumps, including a financing plan for low-income residents and public/private incentives.
dedup2.source_quote: OSE will propose recommendations to the mayor aimed at accelerating the transition of 18,000 homes from heating with oil to an electric heat pump, and adequately serving those unable to finance the switch alone. Recommendations will include a financing plan to support low-income residents, as well as a combination of public and private incentives to spur action. Accomplishing this switch will reduce heating costs and minimize the threat of leaking tanks.
dedup2.extraction_rationale: This is a department-level commitment to deliver formal recommendations with a quantified scope (18,000 homes) and named mechanisms (financing plan and incentives), though it does not state a deadline for the recommendations.

dedup2.policy_statement: By October 2018, the Mayor of Seattle will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with City departments to define which projects to assess for GHG impacts, the assessment method, and how to account for broader carbon costs.
dedup2.source_quote: City policies, plans and major investments have wide reaching and long-term climate impacts.  However, the City lacks a systematic way to assess the GHG emissions associated with major City actions, and to consider the cost of those emissions during the planning process. Creating such a system would help the City make better decisions in the short-term and be prepared for future financial impacts, such as carbon pricing. The Mayor will direct the Office of Sustainability & Environment to work with departments to define the types of projects to assess, the assessment method, and how to account for the broader costs of carbon, by October 2018.
dedup2.section_header: Assess GHG Emissions Impact of City decisions
dedup2.extraction_rationale: This is a time-bound mayoral directive to a named office to establish the scope and method for a GHG assessment system by a specified deadline.

## Extraction
You are a climate policy analyst. Your task is to extract climate policies from a long policy document with high precision (avoid spurious “policy-like” facts).

For each extracted policy, produce a JSON object with these fields:

EXTRACTION FIELDS
- "policy_statement": concise, self-contained commitment that preserves: (a) actor, (b) sector/scope (e.g., municipal vs citywide), (c) action/mechanism, and (d) any targets, baseline, and deadlines. Write it so it can stand alone outside the document.
- "source_quote": verbatim quote (typically 1–3 sentences) that directly contains the commitment. Do not stitch together non-adjacent text. If a policy has multiple key parts in the same paragraph (e.g., funding + target), include the sentence(s) covering all key parts.
- "section_header": the nearest section/subsection heading that governs the quoted text (copy from document).
- "extraction_rationale": 1–2 sentences explaining why it is a policy and noting any missing specifics (e.g., no timeline), or why you split/merged items.

WHAT COUNTS AS A POLICY (TIGHTENED)
Extract ONLY items that are clearly a government (or named agency/department) commitment, requirement, adoption, or funded action. A policy must include at least one strong anchor:

STRONG POLICY ANCHORS (extract)
1) Adopted/approved instrument: ordinance, resolution, code/standard adoption, plan/program launch, executive order, contract, formal strategy with commitments.
2) Enforceable requirement: “require,” “must,” “prohibit,” “mandate,” “standard,” “code requires…”
3) Budget/resource commitment: dollars, budget changes (e.g., “double funding”), staffing, procurement commitment.
4) Quantified target WITH scope: numeric target + timeframe (and baseline if stated) tied to a responsible actor (City, department, utility) and a defined scope (e.g., “City-owned buildings,” “municipal fleet”).

WEAK/AMBIGUOUS ITEMS (do NOT extract unless upgraded by a strong anchor)
- Descriptive status or progress: “on track,” “has reduced,” “currently,” “as of…”
- General goals/aspirations without mechanism or responsible actor: “aim to,” “support,” “encourage,” “work toward,” “seek to,” “promote”
- Explanations of what a code/program is, unless the text states an actual requirement or adoption applicable in the jurisdiction.
- Forecasts, potentials, benefits, rationale, stakeholder/process steps, studies, pilots described only as concepts (unless a launch/implementation commitment is stated).

SCOPE & SPECIFICITY RULES (to improve match quality)
- Preserve scope exactly: distinguish “municipal/City-owned operations” vs “citywide/community-wide.” If the text is about City-owned buildings, do NOT rewrite as “buildings sector” or “citywide buildings.”
- Prefer the most specific commitment over a derived/summary metric. If the document provides an operational target and/or funding mechanism (e.g., “double budget 2021–2025” + “reduce municipal building energy 40% by 2025”), extract that, not a broader “on track to meet city goal…”.
- Include all key components that are stated together: if a policy sentence lists multiple measures or a two-part commitment (e.g., two pilots; funding + target; target + baseline), capture them in ONE policy_statement when they are clearly part of the same commitment. Only split if they are independent actions not linked by the text.

DEDUPLICATION / GRANULARITY
- Deduplicate true duplicates (same actor + action + target/timeline), keeping the most detailed version.
- Do not “invent” new policies by generalizing a described feature into a commitment. If unsure whether it is descriptive vs mandatory, do NOT extract.

STRATEGY
1) Process section by section using headers as anchors.
2) In each section, extract only statements meeting the strong-anchor test; prioritize specificity (actor/scope/mechanism/target).
3) When a section mixes “policy context” with “requirements/commitments,” extract only the requirements/commitments and quote them.
4) Collect extracted policies into a single Python list of dicts, deduplicate, store as `all_policies`, and call FINAL_VAR(all_policies).

OUTPUT FORMAT
Your final answer MUST be a valid JSON list of policy objects as described above.

## Hierarchy
EXTRACTION FIELDS (hierarchy-related only):
- "role": "individual" | "sub" | "parent"
    • "individual": standalone policy, no parent-child relationship
    • "sub": specific action listed under a named parent initiative (e.g. lettered or numbered list items A., B., C.)
    • "parent": umbrella initiative/program that has sub-actions listed beneath it
- "parent_statement": the name or summary of the parent initiative for "sub" role only. Use null for "individual" and "parent".

HIERARCHY RULES:
- When you see a named initiative followed by lettered or numbered sub-items, extract the initiative header as "parent" AND each sub-item as "sub" with parent_statement pointing to that initiative name.
- If a policy stands alone with no sub-items beneath it, it is "individual".

Two-thirds of Seattle's GHG emissions result from road transportation. The Seattle Department of Transportation is preparing a study to investigate possible pricing schemes and how pricing would address an impending congestion challenge being created by tolling in the Highway 99 tunnel, a growing population, and rapid expansion of shared vehicle transportation and urban freight. The single largest obstacle to realizing our climate goals is that the price of fossil fuels does not reflect the true cost of carbon, which is realized in increasing threats to our health, polluted air and water, and damage to property and infrastructure. ## Letter from the Mayor

April 4, 2018

Here in Seattle, we don't wait for others to tell us what our future is going to look like - we create it. We have led the world in aerospace technology, are home to the fastest computers and the cloud, and are pioneering developments to help cure for cancer. And when faced with the challenge of climate change, Seattle is again ready to stand up and lead.

In 2017, when President Trump removed the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement, the City committed to upholding the pollution reduction targets in the Agreement. We know that we are already seeing the impacts of climate change, from wildfires that choke our air to more intense storms that flood our streets. And we know that these impacts are not experienced equally. Around the world, and right here in Seattle, communities of color and lower income communities disproportionately experience climate change.

In response, we must lead with bold solutions that reduce pollution while strengthening our economy and ensuring that the benefits of a clean energy economy are shared throughout our city. Even as our city continues to grow, we must move beyond incremental change and fundamentally reshape our building and transportation systems for a fossil fuel-free future.

Seattle has never shied away from confronting challenges, which is why our City will act and do what is right even in the face of such failure from our President. The actions included here won't be easy and will require all of us to work together to get the details right. But I know that when Seattleites put their minds together and resolve to change the world, absolutely nothing can stop us. We can ensure that our City and planet thrive for our children and all future generations.

Sincerely,

Mayor Jenny A. Durkan

## | Background

In 2011, the Mayor and City Council adopted a bold climate protection goal for our community to become carbon neutral by 2050 and directed the creation of a plan to meet the goal (Resolution 31312). The resulting 2013 Climate Action Plan (CAP) provided a coordinated strategy aimed at reducing GHG emissions while also supporting other community goals, including building vibrant neighborhoods, fostering economic prosperity, and enhancing racial and social justice. The 2013 CAP included a slate of near-term actions - many of which were completed by 2015 - and more broadly defined longer-term strategies to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.

In response to the Trump administration's withdrawal of support for the international Paris Climate Agreement last year, the City Council adopted Resolution 31757, affirming Seattle's commitment to the goals established in the Paris Agreement, and directing the Office of Sustainability & Environment (OSE) to identify the actions necessary to do our part to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The resulting actions, developed under the leadership of Mayor Durkan, reflect a tipping point in the transition to Seattle's zero emissions future. They are designed to move beyond incremental change and fundamentally reshape our building and transportation systems for a fossil fuel-free future.

## |Greenhouse Gas Emissions

A review of Seattle's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions since 2008 reveals mixed results. While emissions are not declining quickly enough to meet our goals, overall, total GHG emissions compared to 2008 declined six percent, while population grew 13 percent, and per person emissions declined 17 percent (Figure 1). The decline in per person emissions reflects the effectiveness of national standards and local initiatives in increasing how efficiently we use energy, in both the transportation and building sectors. However, while Seattleites are relatively GHG-efficient compared to the nation, state, and county, the modest decline in total emissions highlights the imperative that we fully transition our growing city to a zero-emissions energy supply.

Road transportation made up two thirds, 66 percent, of Seattle's core emissions in 2014. Most of these emissions (50 percent of total emissions) were from passenger vehicles (cars, light duty trucks, SUVs and buses), with the remaining from medium- and heavy-duty trucks. Energy used to heat, cool, and power buildings accounted for about one third of emissions, with that total split between residential and commercial buildings. Waste management contributed three percent to total emissions. (Figure 2) Emissions attributed to buildings has declined from about 40 percent in 1990 and 2008 to about 33 percent in 2014.

<!-- image -->

## Changes in emissions since 2008 include:

- Total road transportation emissions declined two percent and per person emissions declined 12 percent due to a combination of more fuel-efficient vehicles and fewer vehicle miles travelled per person as we have increased transit service and walking and bicycling infrastructure.
- Total building energy emissions declined 13 percent and per person emissions declined 23 percent as a result of lower building energy use, particularly for residential buildings due to lower energy use as our codes became more stringent and incentives spurred efficiency gains. Commercial energy use has also begun to decline, but much more slowly.
- Emissions from waste management remain a relatively small component of Seattle's GHG emissions. Total waste emissions declined 14 percent and per person emissions declined 23 percent, primarily as a result of reductions in the annual amount of waste landfilled.

<!-- image -->

Glò

The pace of reductions between 2008 and 2014 helps us better understand our progress to date and the gap to our goals. Passenger transportation emissions declined an average of 0.5 percent per year since 2008. To achieve the 2030 goal of reducing passenger transportation emissions 82 percent, Seattle would have needed to reduce emissions from passenger vehicles an average of 7.5 percent each year from 2008 onwards. Building emissions declined an average of 2.3 percent per year since 2008, which is on track to meet the goal of reducing emissions 39 percent by 2030 (2.2 percent per year). However, between 2012 and 2014 the pace of building emissions reductions has slowed to an average of 2.1 percent, and an analysis of anticipated reductions based on a current business-as-usual approach shows emissions in 2050 only 12 percent below 2008 levels. 1

Emissions from waste management remain a relatively small component of Seattle's GHG emissions (three percent). These emissions declined 14 percent between 2008 and 2014. Because emissions in the waste sector represent a small share of total emissions and have been declining due to a highly effective program of actions in support of Seattle's zero waste goal, this action agenda focuses on the transportation and building sectors.

While the 2014 GHG Inventory shows some encouraging trends, it also demonstrates that there is more work to be done to meet our climate goals. Total building emissions are declining but that trend will slow without decarbonization policies, and transportation emissions have been relatively unchanged over the past few years. The gap between per person total and total emissions reflects the impact of growth and clearly demonstrates that we cannot achieve our goals solely by being more efficient with our resources. Efficiency remains an important strategy to reduce waste and free up clean and carbon neutral electricity to provide the heat and power needed for our growing city; however, we must rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to zero emissions energy in our cars, trucks, buses, and buildings.
